Quick-start of full-scale anaerobic digestion (AD) using aeration
Anders Lagerkvist ⇑, Markku Pelkonen, Tommy Wikström
Waste Science and Technology, Luleå University of Technology, 97187 Luleå, Sweden
a r t i c l e
i n f o
Article history:
Received 8 July 2014
Accepted 16 December 2014
Available online 27 January 2015
Keywords:
Start-up
Anaerobic digestion
Sewage sludge
Food-waste
Methanogens
a b s t r a c t
A conventional 1300 m3 continuously stirred anaerobic tank reactor at the city of Boden, north Sweden,
which was receiving a feed of both sewage sludge and food waste, was put out of operation due to the
build-up of a ﬂoat phase. The reactor was emptied and cleaned. At start-up there was no methanogenic
sludge available, so an unconventional start-up procedure was applied: The reactor was rapidly (8 days
with 1200 kg of total solids (TS) added daily) ﬁlled with thickened, and slightly acidic sewage sludge,
showing only slight methane generation, which was subsequently heated to 55 C. Then compressed
air was blown into the digester and within a month a fully functional methanogenic culture was estab-
lished. The transfer from acidogenic to methanogenic conditions happened in about one week. As a start-
up technique this is fast and cost efﬁcient, it only requires the access of a compressor, electricity and a
source of air. In total, about 16 tonnes of oxygen were used. It is proposed that this method may also
be used as an operational amendment technique, should a reactor tend to acidify.

1. Introduction
At present anaerobic treatment of wastes is going through a
revival in Sweden as it has been identiﬁed as a signiﬁcant and
renewable source of vehicle fuel. A similar wave of interest was
also apparent in the 1980’s, following a hike in oil prices in 1973
and 1979, but today the emphasis is more clearly on the reduction
of fossil carbon emissions and its associated impact on climate. The
number of new plants and digestion capacity is increasing, which
increases the demand of substrate beyond the easily accessible
and easily treatable ones. One likely impact of the present trends
is that operational problems will increase, especially when using
the traditional continuously stirred tank reactor developed for
sewage sludge digestion, and also the need of reliable and expedi-
ent start-up procedures will also be increasing. Well established
start-up measures for Anaerobic Digestion (AD) includes seeding
(Fernández et al., 2001; Syutsubo et al., 1997), dilution of sub-
strates, keeping the temperature stable, gradually increasing the
load and waiting. Start-up times vary a lot but can stretch over
months. A common problem is acid over-load. In recent research
only a few papers focusing on start-up procedures has been pub-
lished, e.g. Zeeman et al. (1988) although it is touched upon in
other studies, e.g. in Ahring (1994).
In landﬁll research, it was found in several studies during the
1980’s and 90’s that methanogenic conditions may be created, in
a large variation of substrates, by aerobic pre-treatment. Aeration
has been applied in various ways, e.g. through the use of com-
posted waste as bottom liners in landﬁll cells or forced aeration.
Stimulating the onset of methane formation was a theme because
the need to avoid acid landﬁll leachate, and its associated transport
of hazardous trace substances, was well recognised. Different
aspects of aerobic pre-treatment were discussed e.g. by Damiecki
(1987), Lagerkvist and Chen (1993) and Spendlin (1991); and it
has been used since in solid waste treatment. A recent example
is Charles et al. (2009). However, this knowledge does not seem
to have resulted in any application in the CSTR-community, which
could be observed in published literature.
Given the opportunity through a full-scale reactor break-down
and the absence of a suitable inoculum, a full-scale test of using
forced aeration as a start-up enhancement was done. The results
including a microbiological characterization is discussed here.
The digester at Swedjans sewage treatment plant by Boden,
Sweden, is a CSTR of 1300 m3 operated at about 55 C. It was orig-
inally designed to digest sewage sludge only, but has over the last
decade been ﬁtted with an additional feed line for various organic
wastes, primarily source-separated kitchen waste. In the fall of
2011, it had accumulated too much irrelevant material (Fig. 1)
from the wastes that it ceased to function.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Inoculum
Due to a long standstill, there was no methanogenic inoculum
left for start-up, only about 1200 kg of TS per day of thickened

and slightly acidic, pH about 5.5, sewage sludge. The sludge was a
mixture from pre-settling and post aeration settling basins, about
equal volumes of each. The total solids (TS) content of the sludge
in regular operation is about 4%, but in order to ﬁll the reactor
quicker a less thickened sludge was used. At the start of aeration
the digester content had a TS of about 2%, and the VS was 70% of
TS. At day zero, the digester had been ﬁlled with thickened sludge
that had been heated to 55 C.
2.2. Experimental procedures
After the desired operation temperature of 55 C had been
reached, an air compressor was connected to the circulation loop
for sludge, at the digester bottom. Initially, 3.33 l per second of
compressed air (7 bar) was added for one week and then inter-
rupted four days due to equipment malfunction. After that the rate
of gas addition was kept at this rate and at day 14 it was increased
to 10 l per second on working hours and 5 l per second during the
rest of the days, i e 6.67 l per second on average over a 24 h period.
From day 20 to day 22, the aeration was held constant at 6.67 l per
second until it was stopped at day 23. The total air addition was
about 50,000 N m3 or 16 tonnes of oxygen (at 20 C).
2.3. Sampling and analyses
During the whole experiment data from the recirculation of the
digester sludge was taken for TS, VS, pH and FISH-samples. Sam-

ples were also taken directly from the gas outlet of the digester as a
complement to the online measurements.
The aeration was maintained by a compressor operating at
7 bar and using indoor air that was entered without dispersion at
the bottom of the digester.
Total and volatile solids were analyzed according to SIS (1981).
The methanogen cell count (MCC) was established by the fol-
lowing routine: A 250 ml sample was homogenized using a Blentec
Xpress model ES3 blender for 2 ⁄ 30 s. Diluted samples were then
ﬁxed with paraformaldehyde and stored at 18 C. Fluorescent in-
situ hybridization was performed as described in Blackall (1999).
A general probe for Archaea, ARC915, was used to identify all
methanogens (Crocetti, 2006). The probes were labeled at 50-end
with an indocyanine dye (Cy3). Microscope used was Diaphot-
300 epiﬂuorescence microscope (Nikon, Japan) with 100 W mer-
cury lamp, equipped with ﬁlter sets (Chroma Tech, USA), and used
with 1000 magniﬁcation. 10–15 ﬁelds of view were counted for
each sample.
Gas samples were analysed in situ using an infrared gas analyzer
(GEM 2000 Plus, Geotech) and in the lab using a Clarus 580 GC
(PerkinElmer).
3. Results and discussion
The results are presented in Figs. 2 and 3. The development of
pH, gas composition and methanogens were used as independent
response variables to observe the impact of aeration and the trends
of all three variables coincide.
The air addition was stopped as the pH of the digester reached
7, and the feed of substrate was started one week after that. The
variable, and fairly low MCC in that phase is probably due to the
digester feed additions, which were somewhat varying and on
the average of low TS-content. However, the difference between
pre- and post aeration are clear. The responses of the pH and gas
composition to the unintended interruption of aeration around
day 8 indicate the reversibility of the process in its early stages.
The aerobic degradation of organic acids leads to the elevation
of the pH, thus making already present methanogens able to obtain
energy and grow. The degradation is also indicated by total TS, and
VS-observations, but less clear. E.g. the observed VS at day 7 was
about 14.5 g per l, and at day 21 it was 12 g per l. The VS/TS-ratio
for the same days were 0.72 and 0.7. However, in spite of clearly
sinking trends over time, the TS and VS data were varying day to
day, most likely due to the small (250 ml) samples used.
It can be noted that the methane concentration of the collected
gas was already about 10% as the aeration was started. So should
the development of a methanogenic ﬂora have progressed regard-
less of the aeration? Is it just a coincidence that aeration was done
at the same time as the methanogens thrived? Experience indi-
cates that it is not (Lagerkvist, 1994) and that there is a dynamic
balance between acidiﬁcation and the development of a predomi-
nantly methanogenic degradation. Also, the trends of pH and gas
composition during the interruption of aeration indicates that a
return towards acidogenic conditions were on-going. However,
the occurrence of methane in a basically acidogenic environment
indicates the heterogeneity that is typical for a three phase system,
there are most often micro-environments available for different
processes.
4. Conclusions
Aeration showed to be an efﬁcient method of establishing
methanogenic conditions in a full- scale AD-reactor. Compared to
the common technique of slow adaption, it is much more expedi-
ent. This technique was applied in landﬁll research and practice
already in the 1980’s, and it has now also been shown in a full-
scale CSTR AD system. It is probable that the technique can be
applied to any three phase system (particles, liquid and gas) as
long as there are microenvironments where methanogens can
grow uninhibited by the oxygen content of the macro environ-
ment. This start-up technique is cost efﬁcient compared to alterna-
tive methods, and it could probably also be used for amending
occasional acidiﬁcation problems during regular operation of
digesters.
